svg.aria-label: Diagram: the four-step Secrets Manager rotation contract, the three staging labels it moves, and the label state that stops every future rotation. Secrets Manager invokes one Lambda function several times with different parameters, passing Step, SecretId, ClientRequestToken and RotationToken, where ClientRequestToken identifies the new secret version and helps ensure idempotency and RotationToken is required for assumed-role or cross-account rotation. The four steps are create_secret, set_secret, test_secret and finish_secret. In create_secret the function checks whether a secret already exists for the passed-in token by calling get_secret_value, generates a value with get_random_password, and calls put_secret_value to store it under the AWSPENDING staging label; AWS notes that storing the value in AWSPENDING is what makes the process idempotent, because a later attempt can refer to the same value. In set_secret the function changes the credential in the database or service to match the AWSPENDING value, and AWS advises three confused-deputy checks first, because the rotation function is a privileged deputy with authority over both the secret and the target resource: confirm the AWSCURRENT credential is valid and abandon the attempt if it is not, confirm the AWSCURRENT and AWSPENDING usernames match, and confirm the host names match. In test_secret the function uses the AWSPENDING version to access the database or service, and template-based functions test with read access only. In finish_secret the function calls update_secret_version_stage to move AWSCURRENT from the previous version to the new one, which removes AWSPENDING in the same API call, and Secrets Manager adds AWSPREVIOUS to the previous version so the last known good value is retained. A central warning records the wedge condition: when rotation succeeds AWSPENDING may be on the same version as AWSCURRENT or on no version at all, but if AWSPENDING is present on a version that is not AWSCURRENT then any later invocation of rotation assumes a previous rotation is still in progress and returns an error, and when rotation is unsuccessful AWSPENDING may be attached to an empty secret version. So the failure is not a bad credential but a stalled schedule on a secret whose credentials still work. A panel distinguishes two pieces of AWS guidance about removing AWSPENDING that apply at different moments: within a rotation the function should not remove AWSPENDING before finish_secret nor by a separate API call, because that can indicate the rotation did not complete successfully, whereas the troubleshooting guidance for a rotation that consistently fails is to clear the AWSPENDING staging label and retry. Another panel contrasts the two strategies: single user updates one user in one secret, is described as the simplest and appropriate for most use cases and recommended for one-time or interactive users, does not drop open connections, but has a short window between the database password changing and the secret updating during which there is a low risk of denied calls; alternating users updates two users in one secret by cloning the first, requires a superuser secret because most users cannot clone themselves, is described as appropriate for applications requiring high availability because an application retrieving the secret mid-rotation still gets valid credentials, and carries the standing obligation that the clone is created with the original's permissions and must be updated by hand whenever the original's permissions change. A closing panel records the operational traps: the entire rotation is retried rather than the failed step, so all four must be idempotent; reserved concurrency should be at least ten and provisioned concurrency below ten can cause throttling, with the symptom being a function stuck in a loop between CreateSecret and SetSecret; mutating API calls on the secret during rotation risk a race with RotateSecret and PutSecretValue; a manual secret update counts as a valid rotation when the next rotation date is calculated; and for MySQL alternating users the clone name is capped at sixteen characters by default while MySQL 5.7 and later allow thirty-two, and because Secrets Manager appends the six-character suffix underscore clone the original username must stay at or below twenty-six characters.
svg.title: Four steps, three labels, and the label state that stops every rotation after it
svg.text: Rotation is a state machine, and the state is a staging label on a version.
One function, invoked four times: Step · SecretId · ClientRequestToken · RotationToken
1 create_secret
get_secret_value — already there?
get_random_password
put_secret_value → AWSPENDING
“Storing the new secret value in
AWSPENDING helps ensure idempotency”
the value now lives only in the label
2 set_secret
changes the credential in the
database to match AWSPENDING
“a privileged deputy” — check first:
· AWSCURRENT valid? if not, abandon
· same username as AWSPENDING?
· same host name?
the only step that leaves Secrets Manager
3 test_secret
uses the AWSPENDING version to
access the database or service
templates “test the new secret by
using read access”
a credential that can read but lost
write permission passes this step
4 finish_secret
update_secret_version_stage
one call does three things:
· AWSCURRENT → new version
· removes AWSPENDING, same call
· old version → AWSPREVIOUS
one request, not three that can each fail
The wedge: a label on the wrong version stops every rotation after it
“If the AWSPENDING staging label is present but not attached to the same version as AWSCURRENT, then any later
invocation of rotation assumes that a previous rotation request is still in progress and returns an error.”
“When rotation is unsuccessful, the AWSPENDING staging label might be attached to an empty secret version.”
Nothing expired. No credential is wrong. The schedule has simply stopped, and the secret still works.
Clearing AWSPENDING: two rules, two moments
During a rotation — don’t. “don’t remove it by using a
separate API call, because that can indicate… the
rotation did not complete successfully”
After it wedges — do. “If rotation consistently fails,
clear the AWSPENDING staging label and retry”
Single user vs alternating users
Single — “the simplest… appropriate for most use cases”.
Connections survive, but a short window where there is
“a low risk of the database denying calls”.
Alternating — closes that window; needs a superuser
secret, and the clone’s grants are a copy, not a link.
The alternating-users obligation nothing enforces
“If you change the original user’s permissions after the clone is created, you must also change the cloned user’s
permissions.” → drift surfaces on whichever rotation lands on the stale user, which is every other one.
Operational traps
Retry is of the whole rotation — “Secrets Manager retries the entire rotation process”, so all four steps must be idempotent.
Concurrency floor — below 10 “can cause throttling”; symptom is a loop between CreateSecret and SetSecret, not a throttle error.
Cross-account — RotationToken is required; omit it and each attempt fails leaving AWSPENDING behind.
A manual update counts as a rotation when the next rotation date is calculated — so credential age is not what the schedule implies.
Don’t write the secret during a window — “no race condition between RotateSecret and PutSecretValue”.
MySQL clone names — 16 by default, 32 allowed by MySQL 5.7+, minus the six-character “_clone” suffix = 26 for the original.
The deputy cannot be chained — “The rotation function can’t call another Lambda function to rotate the secret.”
Alarm on rotation not HAPPENING, not on rotation failing. It reported the failure once, months ago.
The audit: describe-secret across every rotating secret, read VersionIdsToStages, and ask whether AWSPENDING sits on
anything that is not the AWSCURRENT version. Then compare LastRotatedDate against the schedule it claims to keep.
